newsitem.title: UK: Scottish bishop scandal reignites celibacy issue.
newsitem.headline: Scottish bishop scandal reignites celibacy issue.

text.p: The scandal of a disgraced bishop who fathered a love child with one women and vanished two weeks ago with another sparked calls on Sunday for the Catholic Church to review its position on celibacy.

Women involved in secret relationship with priests and a former member of the clergy said the story of bishop Roderick Wright that was splashed across British newspapers highlighted the problems priests faced in keeping their vows.
The 7-11 group, a support organisation for women in forbidden relationships with priests said the church should recognise what is becoming a growing problems and consider changes.

The group named after the day it was founded two years ago on November 7, said it had nearly 80 members and suggested that the number of women in Britain involved with priests could be in the hundreds.
"There are common threads in the relationships in that, to our knowledge, they were all initiated by the men," one member of the group who did not want to be identified told BBC radio.
"Certainly in some cases, women have gone in for pastoral care and the situation has been taken advantage of."

Up until now the group had not spoken publicly but the controversy surrounding the former bishop who resigned just days after vanishing with a mother of three, has pushed celibacy back into the headlines.
"Compusory celibacy, in my view, is in its essence an evil law," Mike Highland, a former priest who is now married and has children, told the BBC's Breakfast with Frost program.

"It is crystal clear to me that if you introduce a law which prevents people from answering the call of God thereby depriving people throughout the world in various countries of access to the Eucharist, that law is an evil law."
It is a controversy that has dogged the Catholic Church for centuries, and one which Britain's Cardinal Basil Hume suggested could be relaxed.
"It is not divine law. It is Church law, so any Pope or General Council could change it," he said shortly after the Wright resigned as bishop from his Scottish post.
The Catholic Church instituted the policy to foster single minded devotion to God and to the ministry, but some priests argue that it is a policy preventing many men from entering the priesthood.
Highland argued that many young men who are taking a vow of celibacy when entering the seminary are emotionally immature, a view shared by members of the 7-11 group.

"It is essential that the Church does not lock these young seminary lads into "you are now out and you have been formed as priests and you have to stay that way for the rest of your lives', it doesn't happen like that," he said.
